dharana.numbering_edition: Jaideva Singh 1979 (dhāraṇā 1 = verse 24; dhāraṇā 82 = verses 105–106 and dhāraṇā 89 = verses 113–114, otherwise one verse each; dhāraṇā 112 = verse 137)
dharana.sanskrit_iast: upaviśyāsane samyag bāhū kṛtvārdhakuñcitau | kakṣavyomni manaḥ kurvañ śamam āyāti tallayāt ||
dharana.sanskrit_source: GRETIL e-text, compared with Wallis's concordance, Pradīpaka and the Singh scan
sanskrit_variants: verse 79: Sandhi only: GRETIL kurvan śamam; Wallis kurvañ śamam, Pradīpaka kurvañchamam.
dharana.rendering: Seated properly on a seat, with the arms half-bent, let one place the mind in the space of the armpits; absorbed in that, one comes to peace.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh translates the arms as 'in the form of an arch overhead' and the gaze as fixed in the armpits, and says the arrangement is meant to put the mind at ease. Wallis and Bäumer read only 'half-bending the arms' and 'the space (void) of the armpits'. This door follows the verse's own wording (arms half-bent) and records Singh's reading.
dharana.instruction: Sit with the arms half-bent and rest attention in the space under each arm.

source_disagreements: Arm position: the verse says only 'arms half-bent'; Singh renders 'arms in the form of an arch overhead' and 'gaze fixed in the armpits'; Wallis and Bäumer follow the verse. This door follows the verse.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition, with one exception that belongs to the verse: verse 79 itself says to sit properly with the arms half-bent; that arm position belongs to the verse, not to the school. That position is recorded in the method as part of the classical description, without any posture name. Everything else about the seat is a convenience, not part of the technique.

points: the space under the left arm
the space under the right arm
geometry.summary: Not a body shape. The map is two small hollows of space, one under each arm, where the mind rests. The half-bent arms only make room for them.
geometry.svg_hint: a simple seated outline with two small open hollows highlighted under the arms
geometry.honesty: Geometry records the dharana's own map of attention, not a body shape. Locations marked 'commentarial' come from commentary, not from the verse.

reaction.name: Rest in the hollows
reaction.summary: School metaphor only: attention settles into two small, quiet hollows of space and the mind comes to rest. Not a biochemical or medical claim.

breath.lands_in: wherever the breath naturally ends; this door places nothing on the breath
breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

orientation.cue: Let the arms rest half-bent so there is a little space under each one
orientation.gravity: Let the floor or chair carry the body completely; there is no posture to hold
orientation.degrees_hint: No angle target: the VBT gives no posture for this dharana

attention.secondary: The peace that comes as the mind settles there

adiyogi.verse_paraphrase: Seated properly on a seat, with the arms half-bent, let one place the mind in the space of the armpits; absorbed in that, one comes to peace.
adiyogi.method_summary: Sit comfortably. Let the arms rest half-bent, for example with the hands resting on the thighs, so there is a little space under each arm. Place the mind in that space and let it settle there. Lower or rest the arms whenever they tire.

honesty.disclosure: Door 056 follows Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 56 (verse 79) in Jaideva Singh's numbering. The door-to-dharana index is a School of 112 Doorways teaching device. Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.
honesty.notes: pairing_type is school_device: the dharana is the content, while the door index, seat and pacing are the school's.
flags: Door index = Jaideva Singh dharana number: Door 056 is dharana 56, verse 79. Other editions number differently (see dharana.numbering_variants).
The seat, breath counts, reaction metaphor, attention-map drawing and beat scripts are school devices, not part of the verse.
The English is a school paraphrase, not a quotation from any translator.
No medical claims. Reaction names are metaphors, not biochemistry.
New door researched on 2026-10-06 on branch research/vbt-houses-2-7; awaiting guardian review.

safety.pain_rule: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.
safety.open_seat_alternate: This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.
safety.contraindication_notes: General practice caution only; not medical advice. If the arms or shoulders tire, rest the hands on the thighs or lower the arms completely; there is no position to hold. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.

beats.title: Breath

beats.title: Attention
beats.script: Place the mind in the space under each arm. Let it settle there. Rest the arms whenever they tire.
